### B.5 · L-0023 — Asset Quality Review

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — worked on one or two government citations.*

`worked` · T1 · banking · reform · 2015-07–2016-03 · confidence high · last researched 2026-07-31

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. 2 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-08-01 (differentFacts, differentFactsNote) · 2026-08-05 (assessmentNote, unmeasured).

**What this is.** RBI review under Governor Raghuram Rajan forcing uniform recognition of stressed assets across banks, ending the Corporate Debt Restructuring practices that had concealed the twin balance sheet problem inherited from the 2004-2011 lending boom.

**What was claimed at announcement.** Force honest recognition of bad loans so that resolution could begin, on the premise that a concealed problem cannot be fixed.

**What can be established since.** Reported PSB gross NPAs rose from 4.97% (March 2015) to a peak of 14.58% (March 2018) on the global-operations basis — a rise driven by recognition, not deterioration. Special dispensations for restructured loans were withdrawn and expected losses provided for. The combined loan book of banks under Prompt Corrective Action shrank around 11% between FY15 and FY18.

**Strongest case for.** This was the precondition for everything that followed — IBC referrals, recapitalisation, and the eventual cleanup all required knowing the true scale. Every year of delay would have compounded the cost, as the 2004-2011 concealment had already demonstrated. The IMF and most academic assessment regard recognition as correct and overdue, and the subsequent trajectory to a 1.8% ratio by 2026 vindicates the sequencing.

**Strongest case against.** The execution was arguably too abrupt. Forcing recognition across the system simultaneously, while PCA constraints bound the affected banks, precipitated a credit squeeze at a moment when private investment was already weak — a meaningful contributor to the pre-COVID growth deceleration from 8% to 3.9%. A more graduated recognition schedule might have achieved the same honesty while preserving credit flow.

**Different facts — flag is TRUE.** The government's case rests on recognition being the precondition for every step that followed, and on the compounding cost of continued concealment. The critics' case rests on the credit contraction that followed and its contribution to the pre-COVID deceleration. Netting the two would require the cost of the concealment that did not happen, which is a counterfactual rather than a measure - unobservable in principle, not merely unbuilt.

**Note on the verdict itself.** Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. WORKED IS ASSERTED ON RECOGNITION, WHICH IS WHAT WAS PROMISED, AND NOT ON THE CONSEQUENCES. The stated object was to force honest recognition so resolution could begin. That is measured and it happened: reported public-sector gross non-performing assets rose from 4.97 per cent in March 2015 to 14.58 per cent in March 2018 on a rise driven by recognition rather than deterioration, special dispensations were withdrawn, and losses were provided for. A measure whose object is to reveal a number succeeds when the number is revealed. THE COST SIDE IS ARGUED AND NOT MEASURED. The case against holds that simultaneous recognition under lending constraints contributed meaningfully to the growth deceleration from 8 to 3.9 per cent; no decomposition separating that contribution from the other causes exists in anything retrieved, and it is entered below as an absence. A reader should take this verdict as saying the disclosure objective was met, NOT that the sequencing was costless.

**Confounding shocks.** The 2018 IL&FS collapse hit as recognition peaked, compounding the credit squeeze and making the AQR's independent contribution to the slowdown hard to isolate. Demonetisation and GST also landed inside this window.

**Not measured — stated reason `never-defined`.** The share of the pre-COVID growth deceleration attributable to the recognition exercise and the lending constraints that accompanied it — The case against turns on this and no decomposition exists in anything retrieved. Separating a credit-supply contraction's contribution to growth from contemporaneous demand, global and investment-cycle causes requires a counterfactual for which no agreed construction exists.

**Series this rests on.** psb-gross-npa, scb-gross-npa, credit-growth

**Measurement disputes this record declares.** P-15, P-18

**Sources** (1, T1×1):

- `T1` PIB, GNPA of PSBs declined from the peak of 14.58% — https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2083695

### B.6 · L-0026 — PSB recapitalisation and consolidation

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — worked on one or two government citations.*

`worked` · T1 · banking · reform · 2015-08–2020-04 · confidence high · last researched 2026-07-31

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. 1 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-08-05 (assessmentNote, unmeasured).

**What this is.** Capital infusion of ₹3.31 lakh crore into public sector banks between FY2016-17 and FY2020-21, alongside consolidation reducing the number of PSBs from 27 to 12 through the SBI associate merger (2017), Bank of Baroda-Vijaya-Dena (2019), and the August 2019 mega-merger of 10 banks into 4 effective April 2020.

**What was claimed at announcement.** Recapitalise banks to absorb recognised losses and resume lending; consolidate to create fewer, stronger, more efficient banks with national scale.

**What can be established since.** The October 2017 package of ₹2.11 lakh crore was the centrepiece, roughly ₹1.35 lakh crore of it through recapitalisation bonds. PSBs swung from a record aggregate loss of about ₹85,390 crore in FY2017-18 to record net profit of ₹1,78,364 crore in FY2024-25, up 26% year on year, with SBI contributing over 40%. No government infusion has been required since FY2020-21. PSB capital adequacy reached 16.4% by June 2025.

**Strongest case for.** The fiscal and operational objective was met decisively. Banks absorbed recognised losses without a systemic failure, resumed lending, and reached self-sustaining profitability within seven years of a record loss — a turnaround few banking systems achieve after a crisis of that scale. That no further infusion has been needed for five years is the strongest evidence the capital was adequate and correctly deployed.

**Strongest case against.** Recapitalisation bonds were fiscally opaque: money raised was excluded from the headline fiscal deficit while adding to internal government debt, with a recurring interest cost, and in substance the government funded banks by borrowing from those same banks. Evidence that consolidation delivered its promised efficiency gains is thin — the profitability recovery tracks the credit cycle and rate environment more closely than merger synergies, and PSBs continued losing market share to private banks throughout.

**Note on the verdict itself.** Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. TWO OBJECTIVES WERE ANNOUNCED AND THEY DO NOT RESOLVE THE SAME WAY. Recapitalisation: met decisively and measured - public-sector banks moved from an aggregate loss of about 85,390 crore in FY2017-18 to net profit of 1,78,364 crore in FY2024-25, capital adequacy reached 16.4 per cent by June 2025, and no government infusion has been required since FY2020-21. Five years without further capital is the strongest available evidence that the capital was adequate and correctly deployed. Consolidation: NOT established. The case against is that the profitability recovery tracks the credit cycle and rate environment rather than merger synergies, and that public-sector banks continued losing market share throughout; no evidence separating merger effects from cycle effects appears in this record and it is entered below as an absence. Worked is therefore asserted on the recapitalisation objective, which was the centrepiece and is decisively met, and NOT on consolidation. The fiscal opacity of the recapitalisation bonds - excluded from the headline deficit while adding to internal debt - is a criticism of the instrument's accounting, not of whether the banks were capitalised, and is left in the case against where it belongs.

**Confounding shocks.** The mega-merger took effect in April 2020, the same month as the COVID lockdown, making integration effects and pandemic effects impossible to separate cleanly.

**Not measured — stated reason `not-published`.** Efficiency gains attributable to the bank mergers, as distinct from the credit cycle and rate environment — The consolidation half of the announced objective. The case against holds the evidence is thin and this record carries no measure separating merger synergies from cycle effects. Bank-level cost-to-income and productivity series exist, but no published study or official evaluation isolating the merger effect was retrieved. **What would close it:** An official post-merger evaluation, or bank-level efficiency series compared against a matched non-merged control.

**Series this rests on.** psb-profit, govt-capital-infusion, crar

**Measurement disputes this record declares.** P-06

### B.7 · L-0029 — Digital public infrastructure: Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, UPI

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — worked on one or two government citations.*

`worked` · T1 · banking/welfare/governance · reform · 2014-08-28–2026-03 · confidence high · last researched 2026-07-31

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. 3 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-08-01 (differentFacts, differentFactsNote) · 2026-08-05 (assessmentNote, unmeasured) · 2026-08-05 (unmeasured).

**What this is.** The JAM stack — Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana bank accounts, Aadhaar identity, and mobile connectivity — underpinning Direct Benefit Transfer and the Unified Payments Interface.

**What was claimed at announcement.** Universal bank account access, elimination of ghost and duplicate welfare beneficiaries through biometric authentication, and a public payments rail owned by no private intermediary.

**What can be established since.** 56.77 crore Jan Dhan accounts by October 2025, holding ₹2.73 lakh crore, 56% held by women and 66% rural or semi-urban. UPI grew from 535 crore transactions worth ₹8.77 lakh crore in FY2018-19 to 24,162 crore transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore in FY2025-26, around 85% of India's retail digital payments, with India accounting for roughly 49% of global real-time payment volume. ₹6.9 lakh crore was transferred via Jan Dhan accounts in FY2024-25 alone.

**Strongest case for.** This is the clearest and most internationally consequential achievement of the period. India built payments and identity infrastructure as a public good rather than a private oligopoly, at a scale and cost no comparable country has matched, and it is now actively emulated abroad. Account ownership rose from 53% of adults in 2014 to near-universal, and the COVID transfer response would have been impossible without the rails already in place.

**Strongest case against.** Exclusion is the cost the headline figures hide: biometric authentication failures have produced documented denials of rations and entitlements, falling hardest on the elderly, manual labourers and the disabled — precisely those the system was meant to reach. The Aadhaar Act was passed as a money bill, bypassing the Rajya Sabha, and the Supreme Court struck down Section 57 in 2018. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 grants broad government exemptions, so the surveillance capacity this infrastructure creates remains largely unconstrained. Zero-MDR drove UPI adoption but eliminated the payment industry's revenue base, leaving the rails dependent on state support.

**Different facts — flag is TRUE.** The government's case rests on coverage: account ownership from 53 per cent of adults to near-universal, and a transfer capability the COVID response depended on. The critics' case rests on authentication failures denying entitlements, and on the constitutional route - passage as a money bill, Section 57 struck down, and the exemptions the 2023 Act grants. Exclusion counts could in principle net against coverage; the constitutional facts cannot share a ledger with account ownership.

**Note on the verdict itself.** Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. THREE OBJECTIVES WERE ANNOUNCED; TWO ARE MEASURED AND MET, AND THE THIRD IS THE ONE THE CASE AGAINST IS ABOUT. Account access: 56.77 crore Jan Dhan accounts by October 2025, 56 per cent held by women and 66 per cent rural or semi-urban, with adult account ownership rising from 53 per cent in 2014 to near-universal. A public payments rail: UPI at 24,162 crore transactions worth 314 lakh crore in FY2025-26, about 85 per cent of retail digital payments, owned by no private intermediary. Both met on their own terms and at a scale no comparable country has matched. ELIMINATION OF GHOST AND DUPLICATE BENEFICIARIES - the third announced objective - IS NOT MEASURED HERE, and neither is its cost. The case against records documented authentication failures denying rations to the elderly, manual labourers and the disabled; this record carries no count of either the duplicates removed or the eligible people excluded, and both are entered below. Worked is asserted on the two measured objectives. It is NOT a finding that the system excluded nobody, and the exclusion question is live and unquantified in this record.

**Confounding shocks.** COVID accelerated digital adoption globally, so part of the UPI growth curve reflects a worldwide shift rather than India-specific policy — though India's starting infrastructure is what allowed it to capitalise.

**Not measured — stated reason `not-published`.** Eligible beneficiaries denied entitlements through biometric authentication failure — The case against rests on documented denials and this record carries no count. Authentication failure rates are held by the scheme operators and the identity authority; a count of resulting denials by scheme, and of what happened to those people, has not been released in any form retrieved. **What would close it:** Scheme-level authentication-failure and fallback-exception data, or an official audit of exclusion under biometric authentication.

**Not measured — stated reason `not-published`.** Ghost and duplicate beneficiaries actually removed, as distinct from savings claimed — The elimination of ghost and duplicate beneficiaries was an announced objective. Figures circulate as claimed savings rather than as counts of duplicates identified and removed, and the two are different quantities; no count on a stated basis was retrieved. Entered 2026-08-05 when the assessment note was written and the objective was found to be unscored. **What would close it:** A scheme-level statement from the Department of Food and Public Distribution, the Ministry of Rural Development or the Unique Identification Authority giving beneficiaries deleted as duplicates and as non-existent, separately, by scheme and year - the holders run the deduplication and produce the counts internally.

**Series this rests on.** upi-transactions, jan-dhan-accounts

### B.8 · L-0031 — Credit composition shift toward unsecured retail

*Selected because: the contested spread — lowest id in one of the seven grounds.*

`contested` · T2 · banking · episode · 2021-04–2026-03 · confidence medium · last researched 2026-07-31 · contested ground: time

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. Never edited since.

**What this is.** Bank credit shifted structurally away from industry and infrastructure toward retail and personal lending, with unsecured retail rising from 22.9% to 25.2% of the retail book and retail loans growing at roughly 24.8% CAGR between FY21 and FY23, about double overall credit growth.

**What can be established since.** The RBI raised risk weights on unsecured consumer credit from 100% to 125% in November 2023 and added 25 percentage points to bank lending to NBFCs, partially rolling this back in February 2025 while retaining the 125% on unsecured retail. By FY2025-26 credit growth of 14.5% outpaced deposit growth of 11.5%, and the RBI flagged unsecured retail, microfinance stress and the credit-deposit gap as the system's principal vulnerabilities.

**Strongest case for.** This is healthy diversification away from the concentrated corporate and infrastructure exposures that caused the last crisis. Granular retail risk is more predictable than lumpy project finance, and the expansion reflects genuine financial deepening in an under-banked economy where credit to the private sector is only around 55% of GDP, far below peers.

**Strongest case against.** It may be risk migration rather than risk reduction — the next crisis would be a household one, and the RBI has noted roughly 10% of retail borrowers missing payments. Deposit growth persistently lagging credit growth is the classic precondition for funding stress, and the fact that the regulator needed to raise risk weights and has only partially reversed them indicates supervisory discomfort rather than confidence.

**Confounding shocks.** Post-COVID consumption recovery inflated retail credit demand, so part of the growth reflects a normalising base rather than a structural shift.

**Series this rests on.** credit-growth, credit-gdp-peer

**Measurement disputes this record declares.** P-19

- `T4` RBI Financial Stability Report coverage — https://abclive.in/2025/07/02/rbi-inancial-stability-report-2025/

### B.9 · L-0042 — Nutrition outcomes and the anaemia reversal

*Selected because: the contested spread — lowest id in one of the seven grounds; put in question by the first external review — contested on a missing-evidence ground.*

`contested` · T1 · human-development/welfare · episode · 2015-16–2021-03 · confidence medium · last researched 2026-07-31 · contested ground: evidence-withheld

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. 1 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-07-31 (caveat).

> **CAVEAT — this renders wherever the record appears and is never truncated.** The anaemia comparison across NFHS rounds is NOT confirmed methodologically sound: haemoglobin testing method may have differed between NFHS-4 and NFHS-5, which would make part of the 58.6% to 67.1% reversal artefactual. Verify against NFHS-5 methodology documentation before citing the reversal as settled.

**What this is.** Between NFHS-4 (2015-16) and NFHS-5 (2019-21), child stunting fell 38.4% to 35.5% and wasting 21% to 19.3%, while severe wasting rose slightly and anaemia in children aged 6-59 months worsened sharply from 58.6% to 67.1%.

**What can be established since.** Coverage-linked indicators — immunisation, institutional delivery, sanitation and clean-fuel access — improved substantially over the same period, while the nutritional outcomes those inputs are meant to produce improved only marginally or deteriorated. NFHS-6 fieldwork has been delayed and its publication status is uncertain as of mid-2026, so the anaemia reversal remains the last authoritative national reading.

**Strongest case for.** Stunting, wasting and underweight all improved, and the improvement continued a long-run trend under a government that expanded the delivery infrastructure for nutrition. Anaemia measurement may not be comparable across rounds if haemoglobin testing methods differed, which would make the apparent reversal partly artefactual. Much of the NFHS-5 fieldwork overlapped the pandemic, when service delivery and household diets were both disrupted.

**Strongest case against.** Anaemia rising by more than eight percentage points in children, and rising in women too, is a large deterioration in the outcome that welfare delivery is ultimately meant to produce, and it occurred while every input indicator improved. That divergence is the strongest available evidence that coverage gains did not translate into nutritional outcomes, and it sits directly against the claim that scheme delivery reduced deprivation.

**Confounding shocks.** NFHS-5 fieldwork spanned 2019-21 and overlapped COVID, which confounds attribution — but the anaemia increase is too large to be attributed to the pandemic alone, and the pre-pandemic phase of fieldwork already showed the trend.

**Series this rests on.** stunting-under5, wasting-under5, anaemia-children

**Measurement disputes this record declares.** P-29

- `T1` National Family Health Survey rounds 4 and 5 — https://rchiips.org/nfhs/

### B.10 · L-0043 — Multidimensional poverty exit claim

*Selected because: the contested spread — lowest id in one of the seven grounds.*

`contested` · T3 · poverty/welfare · episode · 2024-01 · confidence high · last researched 2026-07-31 · contested ground: measure

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. 1 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-07-31 (caveat).

> **CAVEAT — this renders wherever the record appears and is never truncated.** This figure cannot serve as independent evidence that welfare schemes worked. The MPI's indicators are the outputs of the schemes being assessed, so delivery improves the measure mechanically whether or not the output converted into sustained use. See P-26.

**What this is.** NITI Aayog's discussion paper claimed 24.82 crore people exited multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23, with the headcount falling from 29.17% to 11.28%.

**What can be established since.** The claim became the government's principal poverty statistic in the absence of comparable consumption-based estimates between 2011-12 and 2022-23. UNDP-OPHI's global MPI separately reported about 415 million exiting between 2005-06 and 2019-21.

**Strongest case for.** The MPI measures deprivation directly rather than inferring it from consumption, which is defensible and internationally established, and the underlying NFHS data are independent of the schemes being assessed. On any of the available measures — MPI, the 2022-23 HCES reconstructions, or UNDP-OPHI — deprivation fell substantially over the decade, and the direction is not seriously disputed by anyone.

**Strongest case against.** The MPI's indicators are cooking fuel, sanitation, housing, drinking water and bank accounts — precisely the outputs of Ujjwala, Swachh Bharat, PMAY, Jal Jeevan and Jan Dhan. Scheme delivery therefore improves the poverty measure mechanically, whether or not the output converted into use, so the statistic cannot serve as independent confirmation that those schemes worked. A NITI member has acknowledged that a scheme targets each of the twelve indicators. Consumption-based estimates for the same period range from under 5% to about 8.6% depending on method, which is a range too wide to support a precise headline.

**Confounding shocks.** The measurement window spans COVID, and the absence of any comparable consumption survey across the period is the deeper problem — the MPI filled a vacuum rather than winning an argument.

**Measurement disputes this record declares.** P-26, P-23, P-03

- `T1` NITI Aayog national MPI discussion paper — https://www.niti.gov.in/

### B.11 · L-0047 — Railway electrification

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — worked on one or two government citations.*

`worked` · T1 · infrastructure/environment · reform · 2014-05–2026-03 · confidence high · last researched 2026-07-31

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. 1 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-08-05 (assessmentNote, unmeasured).

**What this is.** Broad gauge electrification rose from about 20% (21,801 route km) in 2014 to 99.6% (69,873 route km) by March 2026.

**What was claimed at announcement.** Complete electrification of the broad gauge network to cut fuel costs and emissions and reduce diesel dependence.

**What can be established since.** Delivered close to fully. Indian Railways reports fuel savings of nearly ₹6,000 crore and about 180 crore litres of diesel displaced in 2024-25. India now ranks second globally on electrified share behind Switzerland, ahead of China at 82%, Japan at 64% and Russia at 52%.

**Strongest case for.** This is the clearest case in the infrastructure domain where physical output converted directly into use, because the asset IS the service — an electrified line carries electric traction from the day it energises, with no behavioural change required and no demand forecast to miss. The cost and emissions savings are measurable and attributable, and the achievement is verifiable against an international benchmark.

**Strongest case against.** Electrification was already a long-running programme rather than a new initiative, and the pace reflects sustained funding more than novel policy. Its benefits are also partly contingent on the grid: electric traction on a coal-heavy grid displaces diesel with coal, so the emissions gain is smaller than the diesel figure alone implies. And a fully electrified network that still moves a falling share of national freight raises the question of what the investment bought strategically.

**Note on the verdict itself.** Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 4); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. WORKED, AND THE REASON IT CONVERTS SO CLEANLY IS WORTH STATING: THE ASSET IS THE SERVICE. An electrified line carries electric traction from the day it energises - no behavioural change is required and no demand forecast has to be met - which is why this is the clearest output-to-use conversion in the domain, against schemes elsewhere in this file that count connections rather than supply. The announced object was near-complete broad-gauge electrification to cut fuel cost and diesel dependence: delivered close to fully, with about 6,000 crore of fuel savings and 180 crore litres of diesel displaced in 2024-25, verifiable against an international benchmark. TWO QUALIFICATIONS THE VERDICT DOES NOT REST ON. The programme long predates the period, so pace reflects sustained funding as much as new policy. And the EMISSIONS half of the objective is not measured: electric traction on a coal-heavy grid displaces diesel with coal, so the net gain is smaller than the diesel figure implies by an amount nobody here has computed. Entered below.

**Confounding shocks.** None material — the programme continued through COVID.

**Not measured — stated reason `not-published`.** Net emissions change from electrification, after accounting for the generation mix supplying traction — Cutting emissions was part of the announced object. This record carries diesel displaced, which is not the same quantity: traction drawn from a coal-heavy grid substitutes one emission source for another, and the net figure depends on the marginal generation mix. No net calculation was retrieved. **What would close it:** An Indian Railways or Central Electricity Authority calculation of traction emissions on the actual generation mix against the displaced diesel.

**Series this rests on.** rail-electrification

**Sources** (1, T1×1):

- `T1` Indian Railways / PIB — https://pib.gov.in/

### B.12 · L-0048 — Dedicated Freight Corridors and the freight modal share

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — partly on the same multi-objective shape — the comparison set.*

`partly` · T1 · infrastructure · reform · 2014-05–2026-04 · confidence high · last researched 2026-07-31

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. 1 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-08-05 (assessmentNote).

**What this is.** The Eastern and Western Dedicated Freight Corridors, totalling 2,843 km, were largely completed by April 2026 at about ₹94,091 crore, against a programme conceived in 2005 and approved in 2008.

**What was claimed at announcement.** Segregate freight from passenger traffic to raise speed and capacity, and arrest the long decline in railways' share of national freight.

**What can be established since.** Operational gains on the corridors are real — coal transit on the Eastern DFC fell from 35 to 20 hours, and haulage costs from 95 to 45 paise per tonne-kilometre, with 325 to 371 trains a day. Railways carried a record 1,670 MT in FY2025-26. But the modal share continued falling, from around 30% at handover to about 26% by 2024. Railways told Parliament that the full envisaged benefits would accrue only on further proliferation.

**Strongest case for.** Where the corridors operate they transformed economics — halving haulage cost per tonne-kilometre is the kind of structural gain that compounds, and record absolute tonnage shows the network is carrying more than ever. Modal share is the wrong test for two corridors covering a fraction of the network; the honest measure is performance on the sections built, which is strong. The decline has also plateaued rather than continued at its earlier rate.

**Strongest case against.** The corridors were justified explicitly on arresting the modal-share decline and it did not arrest. Eighteen years from conception to substantial completion, with a ₹2,690 crore avoidable overrun, is slow enough that road freight capacity grew faster than rail could respond. Record tonnage on a falling share means rail grew more slowly than the freight market — which is the definition of losing.

**Note on the verdict itself.** Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 4); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. TWO OBJECTIVES WERE ANNOUNCED; ONE IS MET AND THE OTHER IS MEASURED AND NOT MET, WHICH IS THE WHOLE OF THE SPLIT. Segregation and corridor performance: met and substantial - coal transit on the Eastern corridor fell from 35 to 20 hours and haulage cost from 95 to 45 paise per tonne-kilometre, a structural gain that compounds. Arresting the modal-share decline, which is the justification the corridors were explicitly sold on: not met. Share fell from about 30 per cent at handover to about 26 per cent by 2024, and record absolute tonnage on a falling share means rail grew more slowly than the freight market. The case for argues modal share is the wrong test for two corridors covering a fraction of the network, and that is a fair point about attribution - but it is a test the programme chose for itself, and the record scores it on the terms it was justified on.

**Confounding shocks.** COVID disrupted construction and distorted freight patterns across FY2020-21 and FY2021-22.

**Series this rests on.** rail-freight-share

**Sources** (1, T1×1):

- `T1` Parliamentary Standing Committee on Railways, December 2024 — https://pib.gov.in/

### B.13 · L-0052 — Renewable energy capacity expansion

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — worked on one or two government citations.*

`worked` · T1 · environment/infrastructure · reform · 2014-05–2026-03 · confidence high · last researched 2026-07-31

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. 3 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-08-05 (assessmentNote, unmeasured) · 2026-08-05 (whatHappened, caseFor, unmeasured, sources) · 2026-08-05 (unmeasured).

**What this is.** Renewable capacity rose from 76.38 GW in March 2014 to 274.68 GW by March 2026, with solar going from 2.82 GW to 150.26 GW — a fifty-three-fold increase.

**What was claimed at announcement.** Reach 175 GW of renewable capacity by 2022, later superseded by a target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.

**What can be established since.** Non-fossil capacity reached 283.46 GW as on 31.03.2026 — CORRECTED 2026-08-05, this figure was previously attributed to July 2025, which is wrong by eight months and confuses a capacity stock with the single-day power ratio it was printed beside. Progress toward the 2030 target is broadly on track. The 2022 target of 175 GW was met on capacity though not on the original sectoral mix.

**Strongest case for.** A fifty-three-fold increase in solar capacity in twelve years, achieved largely through competitive auctions that drove tariffs to among the world's lowest, is a structural transformation of the generation mix. Unlike most infrastructure outputs here, generation capacity converts into use automatically wherever the grid can absorb it, and renewable output has grown fast enough that absorption has kept pace with it. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: this sentence previously read 'renewables meeting over half of demand in a peak month demonstrates that absorption'. The 51.5 per cent figure it rested on is not a month and not an energy share — the originating Ministry of Power release states it for 29 July 2025 and gives its components as solar 44.50 GW, wind 29.89 GW and hydro 30.29 GW against demand of 203 GW, every operand a unit of POWER, so it is a ratio of simultaneous readings at one unstated moment on one day. See L-0221's caveat.

**Strongest case against.** Capacity is not generation: renewables' share of energy generated remains well below their share of capacity because of load factors, and grid absorption and storage remain binding constraints. The expansion coexists with continued coal capacity addition, so it has supplemented rather than displaced fossil generation. Discom financial weakness also creates payment risk that has slowed developer investment in some states.

**Note on the verdict itself.** Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 4); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. WORKED IS SCORED ON THE TARGET AS SET, WHICH WAS A CAPACITY TARGET. 175 GW by 2022 was met on capacity; non-fossil capacity reached 283.46 GW against the 500 GW 2030 target and is broadly on track. A fifty-three-fold solar increase in twelve years, achieved through competitive auctions that drove tariffs to among the world's lowest, is a structural change in the generation mix. CAPACITY IS NOT GENERATION, AND THE VERDICT DOES NOT CLAIM IT IS. Renewables' share of energy generated remains well below their share of capacity because of load factors, and this record carries no figure for the generation share - entered below. The expansion has also coexisted with continued coal capacity addition, so it has supplemented rather than displaced fossil generation. A reader should take this as saying the capacity target was met, not that the energy mix changed by the same proportion.

**Confounding shocks.** Global solar module prices fell sharply over the period, which is an external tailwind not attributable to policy; the 2022 commodity shock temporarily reversed some of it.

**Not measured — stated reason `not-published` (stated reason DISPUTED, evidentiary).** Renewables' share of energy actually generated, against their share of installed capacity — CLOSED 2026-08-05, and the reasonKind CORRECTED AGAIN 2026-08-05 because the first correction was itself wrong. The target was set in capacity and this record scores it in capacity; the case against turns on the generation share being materially lower. THE HISTORY, because two corrections is exactly when a record stops being readable without it. (1) The entry originally read `not-published`. (2) A correction on 2026-08-05 changed it to `not-collected`, reasoning that `not-published` asserts something about the world and CEA does in fact publish the datum. THAT REASONING WAS ON THE WRONG AXIS AND MADE THE ENTRY WORSE. The schema's test is whether the DATA EXISTS: `not-collected` means 'never gathered — if the holder were compelled tomorrow they would have nothing to produce', and CEA had not only gathered it but published it, so `not-collected` is flatly false where `not-published` was merely superseded. (3) The schema already provides the mechanism for a stated reason that evidence contradicts, and this case matches its own worked example almost exactly — 'a body saying data was never maintained while another arm of the same government publishes some of it'. So the kind is restored to `not-published`, the reason actually stated, and `reasonDisputed` is set with the contradiction here: CEA publishes installed capacity and gross generation mode-wise on facing tables of its annual General Review for every year from 1950, and its monthly renewable report carries tables titled 'Monthly Renewable Energy as % of Total Electricity Generated' and 'Cumulative Renewable Energy as % of Total Electricity Generated', by State and All-India. The datum was not unpublished; it was unretrieved. It is now carried as series res-generation-share and non-fossil-generation-share and read in L-0221. **What would close it:** Closed — CEA General Review Tables 1.2 and 1.3, retrieved 2026-08-05.

**Series this rests on.** re-capacity

**Sources** (1, T1×1):

### B.14 · L-0053 — Port efficiency

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — worked on one or two government citations.*

`worked` · T1 · infrastructure/foreign · reform · 2014-05–2026-03 · confidence high · last researched 2026-07-31

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. 1 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-08-05 (assessmentNote, unmeasured).

**What this is.** Average turnaround time at major ports fell from 96 hours in 2014 to about 49.5 hours in FY2024-25, while cargo throughput rose from 581 to 915 million tonnes.

**What was claimed at announcement.** Modernise port infrastructure and cut turnaround time under the Sagarmala programme.

**What can be established since.** Both output and utilisation improved together — one of only two sub-domains in this phase where that is true. Sagarmala completed 315 projects worth ₹1.57 lakh crore, with 120 modernisation projects adding about 400 MTPA of capacity. Inland waterways cargo rose from 18.1 to 145.5 MTPA, though declared and actually navigable waterways remain far apart.

**Strongest case for.** Halving turnaround time while nearly doubling throughput is unambiguous efficiency gain, verifiable and sustained, and it feeds directly into the logistics cost that trade competitiveness depends on. It is one of the few places where a physical output metric and its utilisation counterpart moved together and in the same direction.

**Strongest case against.** India still trails comparators substantially — Japan turns ships around in about eight hours against India's forty-nine — so the improvement is from a very low base and the gap remains large. Inland waterways is the weaker half of the programme, where declared national waterways far exceed those actually navigable, and the headline cargo growth there rests on a small number of stretches.

**Note on the verdict itself.** Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 4); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. WORKED, AND UNUSUALLY FOR THIS FILE BOTH THE OUTPUT AND ITS UTILISATION MOVED TOGETHER. Turnaround time halved while throughput nearly doubled - an efficiency gain that is verifiable, sustained, and feeds directly into logistics cost - alongside 315 completed projects worth 1.57 lakh crore and about 400 MTPA of added capacity. That is the announced object, modernisation and turnaround, delivered. TWO LIMITS THE VERDICT ACCOMMODATES RATHER THAN IGNORES. The improvement is from a low base and the gap to comparators remains large: about forty-nine hours against roughly eight in Japan. And inland waterways is the weaker half, where declared national waterways far exceed those actually navigable and the cargo growth rests on a small number of stretches; the navigable-against-declared figure is entered below.

**Confounding shocks.** COVID depressed FY2020-21 throughput; global shipping disruption in 2021-22 affected turnaround measurement.

**Not measured — stated reason `not-published`.** National waterways actually navigable against those declared — The record states the two diverge and gives no figure for the navigable extent. The inland waterways authority declares the waterways and surveys their navigability, so both numbers exist in its hands; the comparison is not published in a form retrieved here. **What would close it:** An Inland Waterways Authority of India statement of declared against operationally navigable length by waterway.

**Series this rests on.** port-turnaround, port-cargo

### B.15 · L-0056 — Mobile internet expansion and the attribution question

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — contested on a missing-evidence ground.*

`contested` · T1 · infrastructure · episode · 2016-09–2026-03 · confidence high · last researched 2026-07-31 · contested ground: evidence-unobservable

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. Never edited since.

**What this is.** Internet subscribers rose from about 30 crore in FY2014-15 to roughly 109 crore by FY2025-26, with data consumption per user rising from 0.27 GB a month to 20.27 GB.

**What can be established since.** The dominant cause was the launch of Reliance Jio in September 2016, which cut 4G data prices by roughly 98% and forced the market to follow. This is the largest usage gain in the infrastructure domain and it was produced by private competition rather than public programme. The public counterpart, BharatNet, connected 2.14 lakh gram panchayats as service-ready but with functional last-mile delivery lagging, at a cost that rose from ₹20,000 crore to about ₹1.39 lakh crore across more than six deadline revisions.

**Strongest case for.** Spectrum policy, the licensing framework and the decision not to protect incumbents from Jio's entry were government choices that made the disruption possible, and the digital public infrastructure built on top of cheap data — UPI, Aadhaar authentication, DBT — is genuinely policy-driven. A government that permits a competitor to destroy incumbent margins in the public interest deserves credit for restraint.

**Strongest case against.** The price collapse that drove adoption was a private commercial strategy funded by a single conglomerate, and attributing it to policy inverts cause and effect. Where the state built directly — BharatNet — the result was a sevenfold cost overrun, six deadline revisions, and a connectivity metric that measures fibre reaching a village rather than anyone receiving service. The contrast between the two is the finding.

**Confounding shocks.** COVID accelerated data adoption worldwide, so part of the FY2020-21 onward growth reflects a global shift.

**Series this rests on.** internet-subscribers, bharatnet-gps

**Measurement disputes this record declares.** P-37

**Sources** (1, T1×1):

- `T1` TRAI performance indicator reports — https://trai.gov.in/

### B.16 · L-0057 — Capital expenditure push and execution efficiency

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — contested on a missing-evidence ground.*

`contested` · T2 · infrastructure/macro · reform · 2021-04–2026-03 · confidence medium · last researched 2026-07-31 · contested ground: evidence-withheld

**History.** Created 2026-07-31. Never edited since.

**What this is.** Central capital expenditure rose from ₹2 lakh crore in FY2014-15 to ₹11.21 lakh crore in FY2025-26, supported by the National Infrastructure Pipeline, PM Gati Shakti and the National Monetisation Pipeline.

**What was claimed at announcement.** Crowd in private investment and accelerate infrastructure delivery through coordinated planning and asset monetisation.

**What can be established since.** Spending scaled dramatically. Execution efficiency did not improve alongside it: MoSPI's flash reports show delayed central sector projects rising from 27.1% of those monitored in March 2019 to 41.6% in March 2024, with cost overruns of about ₹5 trillion, 18.7% of original sanctioned cost. NMP 1.0 achieved roughly 90% of its ₹6 lakh crore target. Private investment remained weak throughout, as Phase 2 established.

**Strongest case for.** Sustaining a fivefold real increase in public capital expenditure through a pandemic, when private investment had withdrawn, prevented an infrastructure investment collapse and built assets that will yield for decades. Gati Shakti's coordination layer addressed a real problem of ministries planning in isolation, and monetisation recycled capital without new borrowing. Delay percentages rise mechanically when the portfolio of monitored projects expands rapidly.

**Strongest case against.** Delays rose by half and cost overruns reached ₹5 trillion during precisely the period when coordination was supposed to have improved, which is weak evidence for Gati Shakti's effect. The crowding-in premise failed on its own terms — private investment stayed weak throughout, as the corporate tax cut record separately shows. Overruns are likely understated because agencies do not consistently report revised estimates.

**Confounding shocks.** COVID disrupted execution across FY2020-21 and FY2021-22, and the 2022 commodity shock raised input costs, both of which inflate delay and overrun statistics independent of management.

**Series this rests on.** project-delays, logistics-cost-gdp

**Measurement disputes this record declares.** P-36

### B.17 · L-0070 — Farmer suicides

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — contested on a missing-evidence ground.*

`contested` · T1 · human-development · episode · 2014-01–2024-12 · confidence medium · last researched 2026-08-01 · contested ground: evidence-withheld

**History.** Created 2026-08-01. Never edited since.

**What this is.** Suicides in the farming sector totalled roughly 112,000 over the decade, peaking at 11,290 in 2022 before easing to 10,786 (2023) and 10,546 (2024). The data are structurally compromised and every level is a lower bound.

**What can be established since.** NCRB separated cultivators from agricultural labourers in 2014, breaking comparability with earlier totals. By 2022 agricultural labourers (6,083) outnumbered cultivators (5,207) — the same wage-dependence shift the Situation Assessment Survey shows. Maharashtra accounted for about 38% of the 2022 total, followed by Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Madhya Pradesh. Several states have reported zero farm suicides in some years, and women farmers are systematically undercounted because land titles are rarely in their names.

**Strongest case for.** The absolute number has been broadly flat to declining across the decade despite a growing agricultural workforce, and fell in 2023 and 2024 from the 2022 peak. Suicide is multi-causal and attributing it to agricultural policy specifically is not straightforward, particularly given the labourer-cultivator composition shift. Several state-level interventions in Maharashtra and Karnataka target farm distress directly.

**Strongest case against.** The data cannot support a claim of improvement because they cannot support a claim about levels at all: states reporting zero are not reporting, women farmers are recorded as housewives, and the labourer category was historically excluded. A series with these defects showing roughly flat numbers is consistent with a worsening reality. And 112,000 deaths over a decade in a sector the government describes as transformed is the fact, whatever the trend.

**Confounding shocks.** COVID and the 2020-21 rural distress period sit inside the series, as does the 2022 heat shock.

**Series this rests on.** farmer-suicides

**Measurement disputes this record declares.** P-44, P-45

**Sources** (1, T1×1):

- `T1` NCRB Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India — https://ncrb.gov.in/

### B.18 · L-0075 — Vijay Madanlal Choudhary and the PMLA procedural architecture

*Selected because: the contested spread — lowest id in one of the seven grounds; put in question by the first external review — contested with a pending outside adjudication.*

`contested` · T2 · governance · event · 2022-07 · confidence high · last researched 2026-08-01 · contested ground: interpretation

**History.** Created 2026-08-01. Never edited since.

**What this is.** A three-judge bench upheld the PMLA provisions on search, seizure, attachment, arrest, the reverse burden of proof in Section 24, the twin bail conditions in Section 45, and the admissibility of statements to ED officers under Section 50, and held that the ECIR need not be supplied to the accused. Review petitions were admitted in August 2022 on two of those holdings and remain pending.

**Strongest case for.** The Court held that money laundering is a distinct offence with transnational reach, that the ECIR is an internal document rather than an FIR and so attracts different disclosure obligations, and that Parliament may calibrate procedure to the gravity of an offence. The twin bail conditions replicate a legislative approach the Court has upheld in other special statutes. The judgment was a considered constitutional ruling on a fully argued challenge, not an administrative accommodation.

**Strongest case against.** The combination of a reverse burden, admissible statements recorded in custody by officers who are not police, and a bail bar requiring the court to be satisfied of innocence at the threshold, inverts ordinary criminal-procedure protections in a single statute. The Court admitted review petitions within a month on exactly two points - non-supply of the ECIR and the reversed presumption of innocence - which is an unusual acknowledgment that the reasoning may not hold. Four years on, the review has not been heard.

**Measurement disputes this record declares.** P-52

**Sources** (1, T1×1):

- `T1` Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India, Supreme Court of India, July 2022 — https://main.sci.gov.in/

### B.19 · L-0079 — Agency action against news organisations

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — contested on a missing-evidence ground.*

`contested` · T2 · governance · episode · 2021–2024 · confidence medium · last researched 2026-08-01 · contested ground: evidence-unobservable

**History.** Created 2026-08-01. 1 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-08-01 (differentFacts, differentFactsNote).

**What this is.** Income tax surveys at BBC India offices in February 2023, income tax raids on Dainik Bhaskar and Bharat Samachar in July 2021, and the arrest of NewsClick's founder and HR head under the UAPA in October 2023. The Supreme Court declared the NewsClick arrest and remand invalid in May 2024 for failure to furnish written grounds of arrest.

**Strongest case for.** Tax and foreign-funding law applies to media companies as it does to any other company, and exempting them would create a protected class. The CBDT stated specific allegations in the BBC matter concerning transfer pricing and diversion of profits, and in the Dainik Bhaskar matter alleged evasion of a defined magnitude. The NewsClick investigation followed published reporting on foreign funding, not on editorial content. In each instance the outlets continued publishing.

**Strongest case against.** The timing in each case is close enough to critical coverage to require explanation: the BBC survey came weeks after a documentary on the Prime Minister, the Dainik Bhaskar raids followed its reporting on the second COVID wave. The Supreme Court found the NewsClick arrest unlawful, which establishes at least one instance where the process itself failed the legal standard. The Committee to Protect Journalists recorded seven journalists jailed in India on its 1 December census in each of 2020 through 2023, most held under the UAPA.

### B.20 · L-0082 — Sedition kept in abeyance, then replaced

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — contested with a pending outside adjudication.*

`contested` · T2 · governance · reform · 2022–2024 · confidence high · last researched 2026-08-01 · contested ground: time

**History.** Created 2026-08-01. 1 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-08-01 (differentFacts, differentFactsNote, revisitTrigger).

**What this is.** The Supreme Court kept IPC Section 124A in abeyance in May 2022, freezing pending trials and fresh registrations; recorded cases fell from 76 in 2021 to 20 in 2022. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 removed 124A and introduced Section 152, covering acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.

**Strongest case for.** A colonial-era offence that had been used against 548 people between 2015 and 2020 with 12 convictions is off the statute book, and the government did what critics had demanded for decades. Section 152 is framed around sovereignty and territorial integrity rather than around disaffection towards the government, which is the narrowing critics had specifically asked for. Registrations fell sharply and immediately after the abeyance order.

**Strongest case against.** Section 152 covers a wider range of conduct than 124A on its face, including by subversive activities and encouraging separatist feelings, and carries a higher minimum sentence. More importantly, 124A had accumulated six decades of judicial narrowing since Kedar Nath Singh, all of which attaches to the repealed text and none of which automatically attaches to the new one, so the effective scope may be broader even if the words are narrower. Calling this a repeal is a description of the statute book rather than of the law in operation.

**Re-test when.** Effective scope of BNS 152 in operation becomes a buildable common measure once a prosecution record accumulates. Re-test against (c) then.

**Series this rests on.** sedition-cases-registered

**Measurement disputes this record declares.** P-51

### B.21 · L-0092 — The Ministry of Education's two framings of ASER 2024, six months apart

*Selected because: the contested spread — lowest id in one of the seven grounds.*

`contested` · T3 · governance/education · event · 2025-02-04–2025-07-28 · confidence high · last researched 2026-08-02 · contested ground: vocabulary-residue

**History.** Created 2026-08-02. Never edited since.

**What this is.** On 4 February 2025 the Ministry of Education issued a factsheet on ASER 2024 headlined 'Leap in Rural School Enrollment' which reproduced ASER's findings near-verbatim while deleting every 2022 data point. On 28 July 2025 the same Ministry published a backgrounder attributing the learning recovery to its own policies - and reinstated the same 2022 troughs, because the recovery cannot be shown without them.

**What can be established since.** Three separate 2022 figures were removed from the February document. ASER: government enrolment among 6-14s 'was 65.6 per cent in 2018. The pandemic saw large increases in government school enrollments (72.9 per cent in 2022). But by 2024, the all-India figure declined to 66.8 per cent.' The factsheet: '...In 2018, 65.5 per cent... By 2024, the all-India figure increased to 66.8 per cent.' A 6.1-point decline from the 2022 peak was presented, under a headline claiming a leap, as an increase - by deleting the peak. Standard III government reading lost its 'fell to 16.3 per cent in 2022'; Standard III arithmetic lost its '25.9 per cent in 2022'; and 'dropped from 13.1 per cent in 2018 to 7.5 per cent in 2022, but stayed about the same at 7.9 per cent in 2024' became 'dropped sharply from 13.1 per cent in 2018 to 7.9 per cent in 2024'. In July, the backgrounder - sourced internally to the Department's own Ready Reckoner - wrote that Class III government-school reading reached 23.4 per cent in 2024, 'up from 16.3 per cent in 2022 and 20.9 per cent in 2018', and that arithmetic reached 27.6 per cent 'compared to 20.2 per cent in 2022'.

**Strongest case for.** A press factsheet is a summary, not a statistical publication, and summarising a six-year movement from 2018 to 2024 without narrating the intermediate trough is ordinary précis rather than misrepresentation. The underlying ASER report was public, in full, on the same day; nothing was concealed from anyone who read it. The figures reproduced are accurate as far as they go, the endpoints are correctly stated, and the enrolment claim is defensible on its own terms: rural government-school enrolment in 2024 IS higher than in 2018. And when the Ministry did make an attribution claim, in July, it stated the trough plainly and correctly.

**Strongest case against.** The February document is not a summary. It reproduces ASER's own sentences near-verbatim and then removes three numbers, each of which is the one that makes the sentence say the opposite of what the headline claims. The headline is 'Leap in Rural School Enrollment' and the underlying movement it describes is a 6.1-point fall from a peak - a leap manufactured by deleting the peak. The out-of-school figure is the clearest case: ASER's own sentence records that the fall stopped in 2022 and the number ticked back up, and the factsheet turns it into a sharp drop by removing the stop. And the July document settles the question of whether the deletions were incidental: the same Ministry, on the same data, reinstated exactly those figures six months later, because the recovery story needs the trough that the enrolment story needed gone. Same ministry, opposite framings, identical underlying data.

**Note on the verdict itself.** The assessment vocabulary is built for measures with stated objectives and this record is a presentational act. `contested` is used on its written definition - the evidence supports more than one defensible reading and the record does not choose - and the mechanism fits, since a précis reading and a misrepresentation reading are both available on the same documents. The value may change on review if a value for presentational findings is added.

**Not measured — stated reason `not-collected`.** Whether the deletions were an editorial decision or a drafting artefact — No internal record of how the factsheet was drafted is public, and none would be expected to be. The record therefore states what the two documents say and does not attribute intent.

**Series this rests on.** aser-std3-reading-govt, aser-std3-arithmetic, aser-out-of-school-15-16, aser-private-share-rural

**Measurement disputes this record declares.** P-59

### B.22 · L-0094 — A national teacher-vacancy statistic, tabled for a decade and then withdrawn

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — statutory duty scored no-objective — the comparison set.*

`no-objective` · T1 · governance/federalism/education · episode · 2014-07-30–2026-07-20 · confidence high · last researched 2026-08-03

**History.** Created 2026-08-02. 3 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-08-02 (unmeasured) · 2026-08-03 (assessment) · 2026-08-03 (asOf, assessmentNote). **Verdict moved:** first filed contested ; contested→no-objective on 2026-08-03 — "Apply the rescore: 25 records to no-objective, 4 notes, 4 held red".

> **CAVEAT — this renders wherever the record appears and is never truncated.** The "10 lakh vacancies" figure in circulation is not a figure for Indian school teaching posts at large. It covers government and Samagra Shiksha-funded aided schools; private unaided schools are wholly outside it, and the denominator is almost never stated when the number is quoted.

**What this is.** From 2014 the Ministry routinely tabled all-India totals for sanctioned, in-position and vacant school teaching posts in both Houses, drawn from Annual Work Plan and Budget and Project Approval Board returns. The last full national figure was given on 02.08.2023 (Rajya Sabha Unstarred 1460); the last vacancy-only national figure on 07.02.2024 (Rajya Sabha Unstarred 525). Since then no answer in either House has carried a sanctioned or a vacancy number at any level. The Ministry continues to compute it: it furnished 63,26,207 sanctioned and 9,59,148 vacant for 2023-24, and 69,85,760 and 9,82,662 for 2024-25, to the Standing Committee on 7 January 2025, printed in the 368th Report of 08.08.2025.

**What can be established since.** The refusal formulation - that education is in the Concurrent List and the data is maintained by States - appears in 1 of 46 retrieved answers from the 16th Lok Sabha and in 37 of about 76 from the 17th and 18th, and its spread maps onto the disappearance of the tables. The source migrated with it: AWP&B and PAB minutes (2015-2019), which carry sanctioned posts, then PRABANDH (2020-2024), then UDISE+ (2025-2026), which does not. A full-text search of the UDISE+ 2023-24 and 2024-25 national reports returns zero occurrences of any form of "vacancy" or "sanction"; UDISE+ holds no sanctioned-post denominator, so no vacancy is computable from it. On 17.12.2025 an MP put the Ministry’s own two Standing Committee totals to the Minister by number and asked him to confirm them (Rajya Sabha Starred 193); the reply neither confirmed nor denied and contained no figure. On 20.07.2026 a question asking for state-wise and level-wise sanctioned and vacant posts (Lok Sabha Unstarred 87) was answered with teachers in position only.

**Strongest case for.** The constitutional position is real and is not a pretext. Education is in the Concurrent List, recruitment and service conditions are state functions, and the Union directly administers about 3,000 of roughly 14.7 lakh schools - about 0.2 per cent. A sanctioned post is created by a state government under state rules, so there is no national definition of sanctioned strength and no national sanctioning authority. The aggregates that were tabled show exactly the defects that argument predicts: "vacant" is an arithmetic residual rather than an observation; the 2023-24 national total silently drops Tamil Nadu, which did not report on PRABANDH; and several annexures build a TOTAL row over 27, 28 or 30 of 36 jurisdictions without saying so. Migrating parliamentary answers to UDISE+ moves them onto a census-based instrument with a published methodology, and answering with teachers in position - a quantity actually collected - rather than a residual assembled from unreconciled state returns is defensible statistical practice.

**Strongest case against.** The Ministry has not stopped producing the number. It gave it to the Standing Committee in January 2025 and let it be printed in August 2025; when an MP quoted those same two figures back in December 2025, the Minister declined to confirm his own department’s numbers. A statistic furnished to a committee and withheld from the House has not ceased to exist - it has ceased to be answerable for. The Union also receives the data as a condition of releasing Samagra Shiksha money through the Project Approval Board, so the federal argument reaches the sanctioning question but not the collection question. And the substitution is not neutral: UDISE+ is the one instrument that lacks the denominator, so the switch removes the possibility of the question being answered rather than improving the answer. The Committee had already recorded, in its 363rd Report, that because the funds are granted by the Union it is imperative for the Department to seek the data and maintain it centrally.

**Different facts — flag is TRUE.** The Department is counting administrative competence - which government sanctions a post, which one recruits against it, and therefore which one holds the record - and the Committee is counting a fiscal relationship, that the Union transfers the money the posts are paid from and conditions the transfer on state returns it already receives. Both are correct and neither contradicts the other. What the record establishes is that the dispute is not about whether the Union can know the number: it produced the number for a decade and produced it again in January 2025.

**Note on the verdict itself.** Scored no-objective, and not reversed. No objective was stated at announcement for a disclosure practice, so there is nothing to score the withdrawal against. `measure` in the reversed definition means an intervention that acts on the world, and every other reversed record withdraws something that was doing work. Here recruitment, funding and the PRABANDH returns all continue; what stopped is an answer. A disclosure practice is not a measure. Not failed either - neither side of the pair describes a failure: caseFor defends the change as competent statistical practice, caseAgainst attacks it as evasion, and neither says the Ministry tried something and could not. The definition of reversed was amended on 2026-08-02 to state this, because this record was its third candidate mechanism in two weeks. VALUE-AND-NOTE RECONCILED 2026-08-03: this record was rescored contested -> no-objective in the pass that introduced no-objective to drain the contested sink, and the note was not rewritten with it, so the reasoning of record argued a value the field had abandoned. Nothing in the validator sees that - both halves are individually valid. The substantive reasoning below stood up and is preserved verbatim; only the value it names has been corrected.

**Not measured — stated reason `not-published`.** A national teacher-vacancy figure in answer to a parliamentary question, after February 2024 — Tabled routinely from 2014; last full national figure Rajya Sabha Unstarred 1460 of 02.08.2023, last vacancy-only figure Rajya Sabha Unstarred 525 of 07.02.2024. Since then every question is answered with the Concurrent List formulation and teachers in position from UDISE+. The quantity is still produced - furnished to the Standing Committee on 07.01.2025 and printed in the 368th Report - so it exists and is producible under compulsion. This is discontinuation of publication, not absence of collection. **What would close it:** A tabled answer carrying sanctioned, in-position and vacant posts, or restoration of the annexures now parked at education.gov.in/parl_ques

**Not measured — stated reason `never-defined`.** A defined national statistic, as against an aggregate assembled on request — No published document defines what "sanctioned" covers, which levels, or which school-management categories. The 368th Report’s entire method note is one sentence recording that the Department furnished the table at a meeting. Two of that Report’s own tables give contradictory 2023-24 totals a page apart - 55,76,000 sanctioned and 8,31,000 vacant against 63,26,207 and 9,59,148 - and it does not reconcile them.

**Not measured — stated reason `not-published`.** The state-wise annexures to the answers that do carry data — Several answers - Lok Sabha Unstarred 4925 of 23.03.2026, Lok Sabha Starred 210 of 04.08.2025, Rajya Sabha Starred 193 of 17.12.2025 - park their state-wise annexures at education.gov.in/parl_ques rather than tabling them. The repository is live and indexed but was unreachable throughout retrieval, so the annexures exist and were not obtained. **What would close it:** Direct retrieval from education.gov.in/parl_ques, retried; if still unreachable, an RTI to the DoSEL Parliament Section naming Lok Sabha Unstarred 4925 of 23.03.2026, Lok Sabha Starred 210 of 04.08.2025 and Rajya Sabha Starred 193 of 17.12.2025, requesting the annexures as tabled. Documents tabled in Parliament are public records.

**Series this rests on.** teacher-vacancy-rate-elementary, teacher-vacancy-rate-ssa, teacher-vacancy-rate-kvs, teacher-vacancy-rate-nvs, contract-teachers-share-government

### B.23 · L-0095 — RTE section 26's ten per cent vacancy ceiling, breached in the Union's own schools

*Selected because: put in question by the first external review — statutory duty scored failed.*

`failed` · T3 · governance/education · institutional · 2010-04-01–2025-12-31 · confidence high · last researched 2026-08-02

**History.** Created 2026-08-02. 1 commit(s) touched it afterwards: 2026-08-05 (sources).

> **CAVEAT — this renders wherever the record appears and is never truncated.** The Committee separately records 'overall 30 to 50 per cent vacancies in KVs and NVs', which could not be reconciled with the dated tables in the same reports giving 17.1 and 29.6 per cent. The tabulated figures are dated, internally consistent and preferred here; the discrepancy stands unresolved.

**What this is.** Section 26 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 requires the appointing authority for any school established, owned, controlled or substantially financed by the appropriate Government to ensure that teacher vacancies do not exceed ten per cent of sanctioned strength. Measured national rates are 14 to 15 per cent. In Kendriya Vidyalayas, where the appropriate Government is the Union itself, the rate rose from 14.7 to 17.1 per cent over twelve months; in Navodaya Vidyalayas it rose from 23.6 to 29.6 per cent over the same twelve months - the statutory ceiling breached by a factor of three. Both readings are at 31 December. The same KVS reports give 13.2 per cent as on 1 August 2024, which is the lower base a seventeen-month comparison would use; it is not used here, because the year-end pair is like for like.

**What can be established since.** The provision was not invoked. None of the four Rajya Sabha Standing Committee reports retrieved - the 363rd, 368th, 373rd and 376th - cites section 26. The Committee argues from adequacy and from 'the spirit of RTE Act' and does not reach for the binding numeric provision its own subject-matter statute contains. The Department's own compliance answer invokes a different measure entirely: 'the overall pupil-teacher ratio of the country is 25:1 across all levels, that is within the norms laid down under the RTE Act' - a national mean offered against a school-by-school duty. Meanwhile the Union filled the gap with contract staff rather than posts: KVS contract engagements rose from 3,260 (2020-21) to 7,909 (2025-26), about 15.7 per cent of sanctioned teaching strength against 8,618 vacant posts, and NVS contract teaching appointments rose 43 per cent from 2021 to 2025 while its vacancy rate rose with them.

**Strongest case for.** Vacancy is a flow, not a stock, and a ten per cent ceiling measured on a single date is close to unmeetable in a system of this size: retirements, resignations, promotions and new sanctions create posts continuously, and a recruitment cycle running through advertisement, examination, result, litigation and joining takes longer than the vacancies take to arise. The central institutions have not left classrooms empty - they engage contract teachers precisely so that, in NVS's own words, 'to protect the academic interest of students, teachers are being appointed on short term contract basis till the vacancies are filled on regular basis', so the teaching position on the ground is materially better than the vacancy rate implies. And KVS and NVS are the most transparent part of the system: their sanctioned, in-position and vacant figures are precise, dated and reported annually, which is exactly why the breach is visible here and invisible for the 99.8 per cent of schools the states run.

**Strongest case against.** Section 26 is not a target, an aspiration or a norm to be balanced against operational reality. It is a statutory duty, expressed as a number, owed by the appointing authority - and for Kendriya and Navodaya Vidyalayas the appointing authority is the Union, which has undivided control, its own recruitment machinery, its own budget and no federal excuse of any kind. It is breached at 1.7 times the ceiling in one and 3.0 times in the other, and the trend is worsening in both, across the same twelve months. The contract-staff answer concedes the point rather than rebutting it: contract engagement is rising in step with vacancies rather than in place of a recruitment cycle, KVS itself calls it a stop-gap arrangement for which 'specifying a fixed contract period is not possible', and it has been the arrangement for at least five years. The Committee's directive to fill these posts with regular teachers 'not later than 31st March, 2026' was, on the Committee's own figures as at 31 December 2025, not going to be met. And in fifteen years no report, no reply and no committee has cited the section: a binding numeric provision has sat unenforced in the governing statute while everyone argued about ratios.

**Note on the verdict itself.** Assessed failed on the written definition - the measure did not achieve the objective stated at its enactment - with the objective being a number in the statute rather than a policy claim. The failure is of the duty, not of a programme, which is why the record is typed institutional.
